rationale: A wins because it treats the causal gap as the story instead of paving over it. Its strongest line, "Chipotle won't raise prices this year — but won't say if the robots are why," is exactly the skeptical frame a reporter can use. B keeps writing headlines that outrun the facts, especially "Its Avocado Robot Explains Why" and "Chipotle Says Its Robots Justify Flat Prices." That is how a decent angle set gets itself sued by reality.
gaps_in_A: "Digital Makeline's testing was disclosed alongside the Autocado rollout, making the two-system pattern visible for the first time" invents a "first time" claim not supplied in the update.
"call it a pilot, not a rollout" is sharp but a little over-lawyered; the update says rolling out to 100 restaurants, so the safer frame is scale skepticism, not semantic prosecution.
The set misses a clean consumer-prices protagonist; the price angle is framed mainly for finance/QSR margins, not diners deciding what lunch costs.
"No clean hand-off yet" is too restrictive. Some angles need proof, yes, but the scale and labor-accountability angles are already fit for targeted reporter research.
gaps_in_B: "Chipotle Is Holding Menu Prices Flat While Food Costs Rise. Its Avocado Robot Explains Why." asserts the causal link the facts explicitly do not prove. The body tries to caveat it, but the headline already face-planted.
"Chipotle Says Its Robots Justify Flat Prices" is invented. The update says prices stay flat and labor-cost figures are not disclosed; it does not say Chipotle justified prices with robots.
"Its Competitors Are Taking Notes" is unsupported theater. No competitor facts appear in the update, and B's own refused list correctly rejects competitor hallucinations elsewhere.

"Labor Advocates Are Watching" and "investor and analyst reactions will surface quickly" are plausible reporting targets, not facts. B keeps mistaking who a reporter could call for what has already happened.
